title: API client class design
idea: The API client design puts one `ApiClient` in front of a `Transport` and gives each changeable decision, retry, timeout and breaker, its own small type.

analogy.text: A courier desk. The clerk takes your parcel, the van is the transport, and a rule card says how often to redeliver.
analogy.breaks: A courier sees delivery; the client often cannot tell if a request arrived.

points: Callers see one method: `execute(request)` returns a `Response`.
`Transport` does one attempt; the client owns the loop around it.
`RetryPolicy` decides whether to try again and how long to wait.
Time comes in through `Sleeper` and a clock, so tests never really wait.

edges.label: takes
edges.caption: A Request is an immutable record. It knows whether it is safe to repeat.

edges.label: returns
edges.caption: The caller gets the final Response, after however many attempts it took.

edges.label: has 1
edges.caption: The Transport sends one attempt. A real one wraps an HTTP library; tests pass a fake.

edges.label: has 1
edges.caption: The RetryPolicy is a strategy. Fixed delay here; exponential backoff with jitter next page.

edges.label: has 1
edges.caption: Timeout is a value object that rejects a total smaller than one attempt.

edges.label: has 1
edges.caption: The CircuitBreaker is asked before each attempt and told how each attempt went.

edges.label: uses
edges.caption: The client waits through Sleeper. Production sleeps for real; tests move a manual clock.

code.title: Types and the retry loop
code.caption: Every type the chapter builds on, with a fixed-delay policy and a fake transport that fails twice.

walk.text: A fake transport answers 503, 503, then 200, and each call costs 40 ms.
Three attempts, 250 ms apart, with a breaker that never opens yet.
Idempotent methods, or any request with a key, are safe to repeat.
Timeout refuses values that could never work.
Four small interfaces: each one is a seam for a test or a new policy.
Ask the breaker, send one attempt, then report the outcome to the breaker.
The policy decides whether to stop; otherwise sleep and loop.

pitfalls: Do not put the retry loop inside `Transport`; then nothing above can count attempts.
Do not call `Thread.sleep` directly in the client; inject a `Sleeper`.
Do not let a policy retry without checking `safeToRepeat` on the request.

quiz.q: What does the last line of ClassDesign print?
quiz.why: Three calls cost 40 ms each and two waits cost 250 ms each: 120 plus 500 gives 620.

takeaway: One client loop; every changeable decision lives behind its own small interface.

starters: Why is the breaker asked before every attempt, not once per call?
Should Response hold exceptions such as connection refused?
Where would authentication headers fit in this design?
